strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: ML-for-CO methods are often evaluated on small synthetic instances, and a benchmark centered on real-world, competition-grade, and very large instances would be valuable to the community.

The benchmark spans a broad range of CO problem families, including graph, routing, facility-location, scheduling, and Steiner tree problems, which makes the evaluation more comprehensive than many prior ML4CO studies.
The empirical comparison is ambitious, covering neural solvers, neural-guided hybrid solvers, LLM-based agents, and strong classical baselines, with detailed per-problem results in the appendix.

The paper provides useful high-level findings: current neural solvers often struggle with scale and distribution shift, classical solvers remain very strong, and LLM-generated heuristics can sometimes produce competitive metaheuristic-style algorithms.
The discussion sections and ablations, especially on whether neural modules help and on Euclidean versus non-Euclidean structure, add interpretability beyond just benchmark tables.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern for a benchmark paper: the abstract and reproducibility statement contain blank availability links, and several solver repository links in the appendix are also missing. Without a concrete release, the benchmark contribution is much less compelling.

The benchmark appears largely to aggregate existing public instances rather than introduce substantially new data. This is still useful, but the novelty and long-term benchmark value depend heavily on careful packaging, standardized loaders, exact splits, and released evaluation infrastructure, which are not demonstrated in the manuscript.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness concerns. Classical solvers are often CPU-only while neural methods get a GPU, but the primary metric ignores time; LLM methods are allowed expensive iterative code search and then run for a full hour, making resource accounting and comparison across paradigms difficult.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, statements that LLM agents can outperform SOTA classical solvers rely on small margins or specific settings, while the classical solver configuration and time budget may not reflect best available tuning.

The training and validation setup may conflate multiple factors: neural solvers are often trained on synthetic distributions and tested on real/competition instances, so poor performance may reflect distribution mismatch rather than intrinsic limitations of the method class.

Best-known solutions are partly produced by running selected solvers for two hours, which can bias primal gaps toward those solvers and complicates interpretation on hard instances without proven optima.

Several dataset choices and descriptions are confusing. For example, the MIS table lists the largest-scale instances in the easy set while the hard set is much smaller, despite the narrative emphasizing hard large-scale MIS; this weakens clarity about what “easy” and “hard” mean.
The ablation study is quite limited relative to the breadth of the benchmark, covering only two representative pairs, so it only partially supports broader conclusions about neural modules.

The LLM-agent evaluation would benefit from stronger controls for leakage and prior knowledge, since many benchmark instances and classical heuristics are public and likely represented in training data or available algorithm descriptions.
Presentation has some rough edges, including missing URLs, grammatical issues, and occasional imprecise wording, which is problematic for a benchmark paper that aims to serve as a reference resource.

strengths: The paper has a useful ambition: collecting harder real-world/competition CO instances and putting neural and LLM-based solvers next to strong classical solvers across eight problem families.

The benchmark includes a broad set of problem types, including routing, graph, facility-location, scheduling, and Steiner tree tasks, and the paper makes a reasonable case that many prior ML-for-CO evaluations are too synthetic and small-scale.
The empirical conclusion that current ML solvers often fail under scale and distribution shift is important and, in several reported cases, sobering for the field.

The paper attempts to standardize training/validation/test resources and reports detailed per-problem appendix tables, which could become useful infrastructure if the benchmark and code/data are actually released cleanly.
The discussion sections ask relevant diagnostic questions about whether neural modules help and whether GNN-based solvers capture global structure.
weaknesses: The claimed public availability is blank in both the abstract and reproducibility statement. For a dataset/benchmark paper, the absence of an accessible URL, repository, license, or persistent artifact is a major reproducibility failure.

The benchmark construction is not sufficiently principled. Easy/hard splits are assembled from heterogeneous sources using somewhat ad hoc criteria, and in several cases the “hard” set is defined by solver gaps, availability, or size rather than a clear statistical or deployment distribution. This weakens the central claim of real-world evaluation.

The comparison protocol is unfair or at least under-justified. Classical solvers run on one CPU core, neural methods receive an RTX A6000 GPU, and runtime is relegated to a secondary metric even though scalability and deployment cost are central claims. A one-hour cutoff plus infeasible=gap 1 can conflate algorithm quality, implementation maturity, memory failure, and hardware mismatch.

Best-known-solution handling is concerning. For hard instances without optima, gaps are computed against BKS that are sometimes produced by the same selected SOTA solvers under limited runs; this can bias comparisons and makes claims such as LLM agents outperforming SOTA solvers difficult to interpret without stronger validation and multiple independent solver runs.

The evaluation of LLM-based solvers raises leakage and contamination concerns. The paper argues hard instances reduce heuristic hacking, but LLMs may have seen benchmark instances, solver code, or published solutions during pretraining, and the paper does not provide a convincing mitigation or audit.

The number of test instances per task is often small, yet the paper draws broad conclusions about “fundamental limitations” of ML solvers. There is little statistical analysis, uncertainty quantification, sensitivity to random seeds, or robustness analysis across instance families.

The ablation evidence is extremely thin: Table 3 uses only two representative comparisons and weak baseline choices, so it does not adequately support the broader conclusion that neural components help only when built on weak heuristics.

Some methodological choices are questionable for a top-tier benchmark paper: training data remain synthetic even though the paper’s thesis is about real-world structure; many neural baselines are likely not designed for the extreme scales used; and adaptation effort across methods is not clearly balanced.

The paper sometimes overclaims. For example, the assertion that GNNs “cannot really capture the global structure” is based on a narrow Steiner-point prediction experiment and should be phrased much more carefully.

Presentation quality is uneven. There are missing links, formatting artifacts, awkward wording, and compressed figures/tables; these are not merely cosmetic because they obscure key benchmark details and reproducibility information.

Ethical and societal considerations are largely absent. The benchmark promotes resource-intensive LLM/ML solver generation and large-scale computation, but does not seriously discuss compute cost, environmental impact, licensing of collected benchmark instances, or responsible use of generated solver code.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap in ML for combinatorial optimization: current methods are often evaluated on small, synthetic, distribution-matched instances, whereas practical CO requires robustness to real-world structure, scale, and solver engineering constraints.

FRONTIERCO is broad and useful, spanning eight CO problem families with easy and hard sets, best-known-solution references, standardized training/development resources, and a unified primal-gap evaluation protocol.

The empirical study is unusually comprehensive, comparing many neural, hybrid, and LLM-based solvers against strong classical baselines across diverse domains rather than focusing on a single problem type.

The results are valuable even when negative: the paper clearly documents scalability failures, distribution-shift sensitivity, memory issues, and the continuing strength of classical solvers. These findings are likely to influence future ML4CO evaluation practice.

The inclusion of LLM-based algorithm-generation methods is a strong addition, and the paper gives useful qualitative insight into when such methods rediscover effective classical metaheuristics and when they are unreliable.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not fully convincing in the submitted manuscript: the benchmark/code URL appears blank, some checkpoint or repository references are missing, and the LLM-based evaluation depends on a proprietary model and API settings that may be hard to reproduce exactly.

The fairness of the compute protocol is debatable. Neural methods receive GPU access, classical solvers are restricted to one CPU core, and LLM-based methods incur substantial development-time compute that is not included in the main comparison. Reporting primal gap as primary while treating runtime only as secondary obscures important deployment tradeoffs.

Several central claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. For example, statements about LLMs outperforming prior SOTA solvers are based on selected cases with high variance, and the claim that GNNs cannot capture global structure is supported by a limited STP experiment rather than a broad mechanistic analysis.

The benchmark construction is strong but not always clearly justified. Some easy/hard splits seem driven by a mixture of size, historical difficulty, and solver performance, and the paper could better explain potential selection bias and why these instance sets are representative of real deployment.

The use of best-known solutions rather than optima is necessary but complicates interpretation, especially for hard sets. More uncertainty analysis around BKS quality and solver-specific advantages would strengthen the conclusions.

Some comparisons to neural methods may disadvantage them because many are used with official checkpoints trained on different distributions rather than retrained systematically on the provided training data. This is informative for out-of-distribution deployment but less definitive about the best achievable performance of each approach under FRONTIERCO.
